# How Ratnasambhava found its canonical form

The ASCII form *ratnasambhava* is not missing anything that this ​name requires. **Ratnasambhava** is the canonical spelling supported by the Devanagari evidence and the tradition's scholarly conventions. This post explains what that form preserves, how it is pronounced, which narratives surround it, ‌and why consistency matters. There are no recovered accents to celebrate; there is something more useful — a spelling whose history can actually be checked.

- **Restored name:** Ratnasambhava

## Overview

**Ratnasambhava** (*ratnasambhava*) ​— Jewel-Born, South · 'Born of the Jewel' — the Dhyānibuddha of the southern jewel family — belongs to the Buddhist tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Jewel-Born, South". The ​name means "'Born of the Jewel' — the Dhyānibuddha of the southern jewel family".

**Ratnasambhava** is the Dhyānibuddha of the southern quarter, the 'Born of the Jewel' whose open palm bestows the ​treasures of the Buddhist path. Head of the ratna, jewel family, he transmutes pride and avarice into the wisdom of equality — the insight that all beings, like all gems, share one nature.

## ​Mythology

The stories of Ratnasambhava place jewel-born, south at the center of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

Ratnasambhava appears in buddhist tradition as jewel-born, south. The name's meaning, "'Born of the ​Jewel' — the Dhyānibuddha of the southern jewel family", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later tradition-keepers preserved Ratnasambhava in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring ​the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Ratnasambhava survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and ‌scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration Ratnasambhava gives the figure a stable name around which these ​variants orbit.

### Born of the Jewel in Akaniṣṭha (The Vow)

In the Mahāyāna cosmology codified in the yoga-tantra canon — above all the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, the 'Compendium of the Truth of All Tathāgatas' — ‌each of the five Dhyani Buddhas began as a bodhisattva who made universal vows before the Buddhas of former eons and attained perfect enlightenment in Akaniṣṭha, the highest heaven of form. Ratnasambhava's ​vow was the vow of giving: to ripen in all beings the capacity for generosity, the first of the perfections (pāramitā), until they too stood as self-arisen jewels. When the vow was ‌complete, he awoke as the Buddha of the south, and the other Buddhas assigned him the ratna family — the line of beings whose affliction is avarice and whose fruit is equality.

​The 'myth' is doctrine wearing narrative dress: enlightenment here is not escape from the world but its enrichment — a Buddha whose very title declares that what is most precious arises from ‌within.

### The South Gate of the Five Families (The Maṇḍala)

The five-family maṇḍala arranges the awakened mind as a cosmic cross: Vairocana at the center, Akṣobhya in the east, Ratnasambhava in the ​south, Amitābha in the west, Amoghasiddhi in the north. Each presides over a family (kula) of beings bound by one of the five poisons and liberated by its counter-wisdom. Ratnasambhava's family is the ‌ratna-kula: those in whom pride and greed dominate. His counter-agent is the wisdom of equality (samatā-jñāna) — the direct seeing that self and other, gold and dust, are equal in emptiness — ​and his emblematic act is the varada mudrā, the open hand. The Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha and its commentarial tradition assign him his mantra, his color, and his throne; Tibetan manuals such as those of ​the Sa skya school describe his visualization in detail for initiates.

The maṇḍala's teaching is exact: the poison of the south is not destroyed but converted — avarice, rightly seen, is the ‌very energy of giving.

### Māmakī and the Wisdom of Equality (The Consort)

In the later tantric development of the five-Buddha system, each Dhyani Buddha is paired with a consort who embodies the ‌wisdom (prajñā) complementing his method (upāya): Ākāśadhātvīśvarī with Vairocana, Locanā with Akṣobhya, Māmakī with Ratnasambhava, Pāṇḍaravāsinī with Amitābha, Tārā with Amoghasiddhi. Māmakī — 'the Stainless One', golden in color, her name a ‌cult-title already known from the inscriptions and art of the Gupta age — stands at the south gate of the maṇḍala as the wisdom of equality in female form. In Tibetan iconography the ​pair appears in yab-yum, the divine embrace: two figures, one awakening. Snellgrove and other historians of Indo-Tibetan Buddhism trace this pairing through the yoga-tantra commentaries into the initiatory maṇḍalas still conferred in ​Tibetan lineages today.

The pairing is the theology of relationship: equality is not a solitary insight but one that arrives, as wisdom does, between two.

## Symbols & Iconography

The iconography associated with ‌Ratnasambhava concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Name** — The restored form Ratnasambhava, carrying scholarly and cultural weight.
- **Domain** — Jewel-Born, South

Symbols ​function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Ratnasambhava across media and centuries. The attributes listed above are not decorative; each one encodes a claim about power, identity, ​or function. The restored spelling Ratnasambhava carries the same precision in textual form.

- **The wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi)** — The ratna that grants every need — his family's emblem and the 'jewel' from ‌which he is born.
- **Gold and ochre** — His body-color: the southern light of ripening crops, wealth, and generosity made visible.
- **The varada mudrā** — Palm turned outward at the knee — the ​gesture of giving that unties the knot of miserliness and pride.
- **The horse** — His vāhana or throne-mount — as Akṣobhya has the elephant and Amitābha the peacock, the south rides on ​energy.
- **Māmakī, his consort** — In the five-family maṇḍala his consort is Māmakī, the stainless one — wisdom of equality in female form.

## A Meditation

Ratnasambhava is the Buddha who asks what wealth is for. Born of the jewel, he does not hoard it: his hand ‌is open, palm outward — the only mudrā among the five Dhyani Buddhas that gives rather than reassures, subdues, meditates, or protects. His teaching is that avarice is equality denied: the delusion ‌that my gem and yours are rival claims on a finite world. To meditate on the south-facing Buddha is to imagine a richness that increases precisely by being given away. In an age ‌built on scarcity mechanics and attention economies, the jewel-born one is quietly heretical: he promises that the wish-fulfilling gem was never a commodity, and that the hand which opens is itself the ​treasure.
